source: Theeuwes (1992) Perceptual selectivity for color and form (as described in Theeuwes 2004, Luck et al. 2021)
finding: Founding additional-singleton task. Observers find a shape singleton (one diamond among circles) and report the tilt of a line inside it. An irrelevant red circle slows search. The cost shrinks when the colour difference is made smaller. Read here only through later descriptions, not the 1992 paper itself.
numbers: Slowing from an irrelevant colour singleton; size depends on its salience relative to the target. Exact 1992 ms values not read.
limits: Original paper not opened. Only the design and conclusion are second-hand.
agent_relevance: Template for a planted-distractor test: a vivid but irrelevant item present vs absent, same task, compare accuracy and time.

source: Folk, Remington & Johnston (1992) Involuntary covert orienting is contingent on attentional control settings (as described in Luck et al. 2021 and search summaries)
finding: Spatial-cueing paradigm. An irrelevant cue before the target captures attention only if its property matches what the observer is searching for. Colour cues cued colour targets but not onset targets. Onset cues cued onset targets but not colour targets.
numbers: Cue-target interval about 150 ms in the classic design. Exact validity-effect ms not read in the original.
quote: Stimuli not exhibiting these properties will not involuntarily summon attention
limits: Original not opened. Two caveats in the original (Luck 2021): with no task a default setting may pull attention; a fully known target location blocks capture.
agent_relevance: A planted hint hurts most when it matches what the agent is already looking for (a number format, a named entity). Match to the task set is the main gate.

source: Luck, Gaspelin, Folk, Remington & Theeuwes (2021) Progress toward resolving the attentional capture debate. Visual Cognition 29:1-21
finding: Joint paper by the main opponents. Two shared statements: (1) salient items such as onsets and colour singletons automatically produce a priority signal and capture attention when no control setting stops them; (2) capture can be prevented when the control system is set up right. The stimulus-driven side now allows proactive feature weighting that cannot beat moderate or high salience. Authors drop the words top-down and bottom-up.
numbers: No single experiment. Debate ran over 25 years. Three groups: contingent capture (Folk, Remington), stimulus-driven (Theeuwes), signal suppression (Luck, Gaspelin).
limits: Remaining disagreement: whether goals and selection history act proactively on feature gain before salience is computed, and whether goals and learning form one control state. Commentaries (Lamy; Anderson) say the capture / no-capture split is itself too coarse.
agent_relevance: Best summary of the field. For our agent the lesson: planted material gets a priority signal for free; what matters is whether a control setting is in place to suppress it before it is used.

source: Luck et al. (2021): original formulations of the two theories
finding: Contingent hypothesis (Folk 1992 p.1041): capture only when the cue matches the control setting, salient or not. Stimulus-driven hypothesis (Theeuwes 1993 p.109): the most salient item wins the first shift of attention, independent of strategy; the one exception is that salience is computed only inside the spatial attentional window.
numbers: Two methodological problems named: no independent measure of the control setting a task induces; no direct measure of whether attention was really captured (fast reorienting hides it in cueing designs).
limits: Both theories were later modified; see later lines on suppression and statistical learning.
agent_relevance: Warns that a null effect of a distractor on accuracy does not prove it was ignored: it may have pulled the model and been dropped. Measure the intermediate step, not only the final answer.

source: Theeuwes (2004) Top-down search strategies cannot override attentional capture. Psychon Bull Rev 11:65-70
finding: Replicates the Bacon and Egeth (1994) design with several shape singletons, but with larger displays (12 or 20 items). The colour singleton still interferes. With small displays (5 or 9 items) it does not, and search becomes partly serial. Salience, not search mode, explains the pattern.
numbers: Exp 1: N=8, 128 practice + 128 test trials. Distractor present 950 ms vs absent 885 ms (65 ms cost), F(1,7)=37.1. No display-size effect, slopes near 0 (about 0.55 and 0.38 ms/item; minus sign lost in text). Exp 2: N=8, set sizes 5 and 9. No distraction effect (F<1). Slopes 13.1 vs 11.1 ms/item. Error 7.4%.
limits: Very small samples (N=8). Rests on the claim that serial search shrinks the attentional window, so distractors outside it are ignored.
agent_relevance: Protection against a planted item may depend on the task forcing narrow, item-by-item reading. Easy whole-context tasks leave the model more open to the distractor.

source: Bacon & Egeth (1994) Goal-directed guidance of attention: evidence from conjunctive visual search (as described in Theeuwes 2004)
finding: Replicated Theeuwes 1992. Then added different shapes (squares, triangles) so the target was no longer the only odd shape. The colour singleton no longer interfered, even in blocks with a single shape singleton. Authors proposed singleton-detection mode vs feature-search mode.
numbers: Slopes up to 11.5 ms/item in the non-interfering conditions, always above zero (per Theeuwes 2004). Original numbers not read.
quote: goal directed selection of a specific known featural singleton identity may override stimulus-driven capture
limits: Original not opened. Theeuwes (2004) argues the slopes show partly serial search, so a narrow attention window, not a chosen strategy.
agent_relevance: The strategy route to protection: if the model is told exactly what feature to look for, it may skip salient but wrong items. An exact target description is a cheap guardrail.

source: Theeuwes, Kramer & Kingstone (2004) Attentional capture modulates perceptual sensitivity. Psychon Bull Rev 11:551-554
finding: Moves from reaction time to signal detection. A brief display (116 ms, then mask) with a colour distractor lowers detection of the target line. The loss is strongest when the distractor is next to the target. So capture changes sensory gain, not only response time.
numbers: N=14 analysed (15 tested, one dropped for d' below 0.70). 864 test trials over 2 days. d' no distractor 1.52 vs distractor 1.37; near distractor 1.30, far distractor 1.46 (no effect). d' test F(1,13)=6.67, p<.05. Hit rate .797 vs .788; false alarms .260 vs .295.
limits: Small effect (d' drop 0.15 overall). Line length was staircased to hold accuracy near 75%. The distance pattern is odd for pure capture, so authors add a salience account.
agent_relevance: Capture can lower the quality of processing of the true target, not just delay it. A planted item may degrade reading of the real item even when the answer path looks normal.

source: Theeuwes & Chen (2005) Attentional capture and inhibition (of return): the effect on perceptual sensitivity. Percept Psychophys 67:1305-1312
finding: Direct evidence of capture. A red distractor flashes 60 ms, then the target display (130 ms). When the target lands where the distractor was, detection is far better. Later it falls, which fits inhibition of return. Repeated with an extra unique shape, so singleton-detection mode cannot be the cause.
numbers: Exp 1: N=8, 1,008 trials. d' at distractor location 2.626 vs no-distractor 1.556; other distances 1.391, 1.505, 1.629. Total exposure 190 ms (too short for eye movements). Exp 2 same pattern with a square added. No sensitivity drop at the target when the distractor was elsewhere.
limits: N=8. Authors note the missing drop at non-target locations conflicts with their own 2004 result and blame the very brief distractor (60 ms).
agent_relevance: Shows the first sweep goes to the salient item. First-pass weight to the planted item, then possible correction later, so an early draft is more at risk than a revised one.

source: Folk & Remington (1998) Selectivity in attentional capture by featural singletons (NASA report copy, Appendix A)
finding: Four experiments with a spatial-cueing variant. Even when the target is a singleton, an irrelevant singleton shows spatial capture only if it has the same colour as the target. A different-colour singleton still slows responses, but with no location effect. Authors call this a non-spatial filtering cost, which may explain earlier evidence for automatic capture.
numbers: Exp 2: different-colour distractor cost 26 ms vs no distractor, F(1,22)=4.76, p<.05. Exp 4: distractor-target SOA 50/100/150 ms. Distraction at 100 ms F(1,23)=9.49 and 150 ms F(1,23)=13.47, none at 50 ms (F<1). Location effect absent at all SOAs.
limits: This is the NASA final-report copy of the paper; wording may differ from the journal. Slowing can mean filtering cost rather than an attention shift.
agent_relevance: Separates two harms from a planted item: pulling attention (needs a match) and a general filtering cost (any odd item). Test both in the agent: matched hints vs mismatched hints.

source: Folk, Leber & Egeth (2008) Top-down control settings and the attentional blink: evidence for nonspatial contingent capture. Visual Cognition 16:616-642
finding: Extends contingent capture to time. In a letter stream, a brief colour change of a surrounding box hurts later report of the coloured target only when the box colour matches the target colour. Control settings can be tuned to one colour or generalised to any coloured item.
numbers: Exp 1: N=38. Distractor condition F(2,72)=66.10, p<.0001; condition by lag F(14,504)=8.27. Same-colour distractor differed from both no-distractor and different-colour at every lag; the latter two did not differ. Exp 2: N=23, mixed red/green targets; distractor F(2,44)=5.23, p<.01, interaction F(14,308)=3.23, p<.001.
limits: Authors also rule out masking and illusory-target accounts in Exp 2-3 (not read in detail).
agent_relevance: Capture works in time-ordered streams, a closer analogue to token sequences than a spatial display. A match with the target format causes a blink-like loss on what follows.

source: Gaspelin, Leonard & Luck (2015) Direct evidence for active suppression of salient-but-irrelevant sensory inputs. Psychol Sci 26:1740-1750
finding: Capture-probe method: on 30% of trials letters flash inside the shapes and observers report them. When the task invites singleton detection, probe letters at the colour singleton are recalled better (capture). When the task forces search for one exact shape, they are recalled worse than at ordinary distractors: active suppression below baseline.
numbers: N=24 per experiment. Exp 1 (singleton-detection): search RT 739 vs 674 ms (65 ms cost), t(23)=11; probe recall 26.6% at singleton vs 14.7% at other distractors; target-location recall 12% lower with singleton. Exp 2 (feature search): RT 667 vs 678 ms; recall 9.6% at singleton vs 15.4%. Exp 3 (set size 4): RT 630 vs 652 ms (22 ms benefit); recall 15.5% vs 27.9% (about 12% suppression).
limits: Probe came 200 ms after search onset in Exp 2-3, so fast capture could be missed; a simultaneous-probe experiment followed (RT 630 vs 647 ms).
agent_relevance: Strong support that a clear, specific target description can turn a distractor from a lure into something actively pushed away. Argues for exact-target restatement as a first step.

source: Luck et al. (2021) summary of oculomotor and ERP evidence for signal suppression (Gaspelin et al. 2017, 2019; Gaspelin & Luck 2018; Sawaki & Luck 2010)
finding: With search for one known shape among varied shapes, the first saccade lands on the colour singleton less often than on an average distractor. ERP shows a PD (suppression) not an N2pc (capture) for the singleton. When the target shape varies so singleton detection is needed, the first saccade lands on the singleton more than on average.
numbers: Direction of effect only; exact fixation percentages are in the cited papers, not read here. Controls: same time to reach target on singleton-absent trials in both tasks; singleton and target locations randomised.
limits: Cited papers not opened. Stimulus-driven proponents (Wang & Theeuwes 2020) dispute the feature-search interpretation.
agent_relevance: Same salience signal, opposite outcome depending on task set. Evidence for a guardrail that sets the target description before reading, rather than hoping to reject distractors later.

source: Wang & Theeuwes (2018) Statistical regularities modulate attentional capture independent of search strategy. Atten Percept Psychophys 80:1763-1774
finding: A colour distractor appears more often at one location (65% of distractor trials there; each of seven others 5%). Observers learn to suppress that location, even in feature-search displays. Capture there is smaller; the target is also harder to find there. Learned probability of distractor colour had no measurable effect.
numbers: Distractor present on 66% of trials in Exp 1; N=24 per experiment. Residual capture of 14 ms at low-probability locations in Exp 1 despite feature search. Exp 2 (diamond among varied shapes) RTs about 1,200 ms, near-serial search.
limits: Suppression is spatial and feature-blind, with a distance gradient. Exact RT values for the high-probability location not extracted here.
agent_relevance: Repeated exposure to where lures appear lets the system down-weight a place, not a feature. A scaffold that marks a fixed prompt region (a hints block) as low-weight could mimic this.

source: Anderson, Laurent & Yantis (2011) Value-driven attentional capture. PNAS 108:10367-10371
finding: Colours that earned reward during training capture attention later, even when irrelevant and the reward is gone. Capture is independent of goals and of physical salience. A third source of control beyond top-down and bottom-up.
numbers: Test-phase cost of high-reward distractor vs none: Exp 1 N=26, 16 ms (low-reward 8 ms); Exp 3 N=24, 15 ms after 240 training trials; retest 4-21 days later N=19, 16 ms. Exp 2 (no reward in training) N=10, no effect, t(9)=-0.39.
limits: Effects of about 15 ms are small. The no-reward control had only N=10. Table values are as computed by the fetch tool from the paper's Table 1.
agent_relevance: A learned association (a token or number that earlier paid off) can pull the agent regardless of the current goal. Relevant to memory and reuse of earlier answers in a scaffold.

source: Awh, Belopolsky & Theeuwes (2012) Top-down versus bottom-up attentional control: a failed theoretical dichotomy. Trends Cogn Sci 16:437-443
finding: Argues the two-way split cannot explain selection history (priming) or reward effects, which are neither goal nor salience. Proposes one priority map integrating current goals, physical salience and selection history. Example: Wolfe et al. found pure blocks about 80 ms faster than mixed blocks with identical displays, but priming could explain it as well as goals.
numbers: Wolfe et al. mixed vs pure blocks: about 80 ms. Reward-linked stimuli capture even when equally salient and against goals.
limits: A review; experiments summarised from cited papers.
agent_relevance: Our agent's prior turns act as selection history. Text read earlier gets extra priority even if the task has moved on, so stale context needs clearing, not just ignoring.

source: Anderson (2021) Time to stop calling it attentional capture. Visual Cognition (commentary on Luck et al.)
finding: Argues the debate rests on a false yes/no split. Priority is a continuous, time-unfolding computation across regions, so the question whether attention was captured is arbitrary. Suggests studying how priority is computed from goals, salience and history together.
numbers: Argument piece, no new data.
limits: Opinion; only the abstract and first page were read.
agent_relevance: Treat distraction as a graded weight on content, not an on/off event. Measure the shift in answer probability, not only flips.

source: Itti, Koch & Niebur (1998) A model of saliency-based visual attention for rapid scene analysis. IEEE PAMI 20:1254-1259
finding: The standard computational bottom-up model. Image features (intensity, colour opponents, four orientations) are computed across 9 Gaussian-pyramid scales, passed through centre-surround differences, normalised so that maps with one strong peak win, and summed into one saliency map. A winner-take-all network picks the most salient location; local inhibition of return then moves the focus on.
numbers: 42 feature maps combined. Centre scale c in {2,3,4}, surround s=c+d with d in {3,4}. Normalisation multiplies a map by (M-m)^2 (M = global maximum, m = mean of other local maxima). First attended location at 92 ms simulated time in the example. Pop-out targets (orientation, colour, intensity, size) were always attended first regardless of distractor count; conjunction targets took time rising linearly with distractors. Natural-scene contrast factor fell from 2.5 at first attended location to 1.6.
limits: Purely bottom-up, no goals. Evaluation on natural images is hard because no objective reference exists.
agent_relevance: Gives a concrete form for salience: an item unique in its local group scores high. For text, a number or hint that differs in style from its neighbours is the analogue.

source: Koch & Ullman (1985) saliency map and winner-take-all (as described in the Theeuwes viewpoint in Luck et al. 2021)
finding: Origin of the saliency map: a 2D map where neurons compete and one winner holds the most salient element. Theeuwes builds his stimulus-driven account on it: salience is computed automatically, independent of task, within the attentional window.
numbers: No numbers. Theory.
limits: Original not read. Known only as cited in Luck et al. 2021.
agent_relevance: Winner-take-all reads out one location at a time. The analogy is a single dominant path that a salient plant can seize in the first step.

source: Wolfe (2021) Guided Search 6.0: an updated model of visual search. Psychon Bull Rev 28:1060-1092
finding: Priority map built from five guidance sources: top-down feature, bottom-up feature, prior history (priming), reward, and scene syntax and meaning. Attention goes to the peak about 20 times per second. Capture paradigms are better seen as bumps in the landscape than as a grab of a spotlight. Bottom-up salience may fade after display onset.
numbers: About 20 selections per second. Recognition (binding) modelled as a diffusion process taking more than 150 ms per item, so several items are processed at once. A salient red distractor slows search more than an equally salient vertical one.
limits: A simulation model; fits to specific data sets (e.g. Wolfe & VanWert 2010) not extracted.
agent_relevance: A blueprint for a scaffold: separate numeric weights for goal match, salience, recency and prior reward, summed by code into one ranking.

source: Yantis & Jonides (1984) Abrupt visual onsets and selective attention: evidence from visual search. JEP:HPP 10:601-621 (from search summary)
finding: Placeholder preview, then letters appear. A target that appears as a new onset is found with a flat set-size slope; a target made by removing placeholder lines (offset) shows steep slopes. Taken as evidence that abrupt onsets capture attention automatically.
numbers: Exact slopes not retrieved.
limits: Not opened. Yantis and Jonides (1990) later found onsets do not necessarily capture against observer intentions.
agent_relevance: Earliest strong bottom-up claim: sudden change. In text terms: a late-added or oddly placed sentence.

source: Yantis (1993) vs Folk et al. (1992) and Leber (2010), Bichot & Schall (2002): the neutral-state compromise (as given in the Folk and Remington viewpoint, Luck et al. 2021)
finding: Yantis argued abrupt onset is special and captures regardless of set. Folk and Remington answer that other properties (colour) capture too, only when matching the set, and accept that salient stimuli capture when no set is in place (neutral state). Leber (2010) fMRI: capture occurred only with low pre-trial prefrontal activity. Bichot and Schall (2002) macaque FEF: enhanced firing to target features and suppressed firing to salient distractors in the receptive field.
numbers: No numbers beyond direction of effects.
limits: Leber (2010) and Bichot & Schall (2002) known only through Luck et al.'s text.
agent_relevance: A weak or absent task set is where planted content wins. Set the task and answer format clearly before any context is read.

source: Luck et al. (2021): Theeuwes viewpoint on statistical learning and reactive control
finding: Stimulus-driven account revised. Salience is still computed automatically inside the attentional window, but learned expectations about where distractors appear change spatial weights. Learning also raises weights where targets are likely. A fast reactive process lets observers disengage from a place learned to be irrelevant.
numbers: In Wang & Theeuwes 2018a (cited there), capture was smaller at the high-probability distractor location; the target was slower there in no-distractor trials; suppression falls off with distance from that location.
limits: Contingent camp says suppression need not be spatial or feature-blind (Stilwell et al. 2019 show feature-based cases).
agent_relevance: Learned layout statistics can down-weight a region. A scaffold can place hints in a fixed region and mark it, then audit whether the model still lets it move answers.

source: Luck et al. (2021): Folk and Remington viewpoint, updates to contingent capture
finding: Contingent capture began as a statement of necessary conditions and stays neutral on mechanism, but allows up- or down-weighting of inputs to the priority map. Folk 1992 p.1043 already said control settings reflect goals plus past experience, so selection history is not outside the theory.
numbers: No new numbers.
limits: Neutral wording lets the theory absorb many results; critics say this makes it hard to falsify.
agent_relevance: Our own evidence should state a prediction in advance, e.g. which hint types move the answer, so the theory cannot absorb every outcome.

source: Theeuwes, Atchley & Kramer (2000) time course of capture (as described in Theeuwes & Chen 2005 and Folk & Remington 1998)
finding: A colour singleton shown at various SOAs before the target display slows responses at short SOAs but not beyond about 100 ms. Attention is captured and then recovers within about 150 ms, which can hide capture in cueing designs that use 150 ms intervals.
numbers: SOAs 50, 100, 150, 200, 250, 300 ms in the original; effect only at 50 and 100 ms (as reported second-hand).
limits: Second-hand from the 2005 paper's introduction. Original not opened. This is Theeuwes' reply to Folk's 150 ms cue-target interval.
agent_relevance: Capture can be brief. A late self-check might not see a hint's effect because the pull already acted early.

source: Folk, Remington & Wright (1994) Structure of attentional control: contingent capture by apparent motion, abrupt onset and color (search summary)
finding: Extends contingent capture to apparent motion, onset and colour. Control settings were found to be limited to the dynamic versus static discontinuity distinction. Found by search; not opened.
numbers: No numbers retrieved.
limits: Not opened; abstract-level description from a search summary.
agent_relevance: Control sets are coarse: tell the agent the category of what to look for, not only the single item.

source: Remington, Folk & McLean (2001) Contingent attentional capture or delayed allocation of attention? Percept Psychophys (search summary)
finding: Tests the rival reading that cueing effects reflect slow voluntary reallocation instead of true capture. Authors conclude the costs and benefits in spatial cueing reflect on-line capture.
numbers: No numbers retrieved.
limits: Only the search summary seen.
agent_relevance: Distinguishes quick pull from slow strategic response; our checks should separate early drift from late deliberate change.

source: Theeuwes (2018) fast vs slow dichotomy, Awh et al. reply, Egeth (2018) (search summary)
finding: Theeuwes proposes a fast-versus-slow split replacing top-down vs bottom-up, with top-down control seen as slow and volitional. Awh and colleagues reply that this conflicts with existing data. Egeth argues top-down is a broad class that already includes selection history.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Only the search listing text was read.
agent_relevance: Two timescales for our agent: a fast pass where salience wins, and a slower code-controlled pass that can override it.

source: Luck et al. (2021): common framework model (Figure 2) and mechanisms of control
finding: All three theories can be drawn in one diagram: sensory register, feature maps, saliency computations, a priority map, with explicit goals and implicit learning acting reactively on the map. Disagreements: proactive gain control of nonspatial features before saliency is computed, and whether goals and learning are one control state.
numbers: Proactive control = boosting features before onset; reactive control = boosting or suppressing locations after the first allocation.
limits: A box diagram, not a fitted model.
agent_relevance: Maps onto a scaffold: proactive control = instructions placed before the context; reactive control = code-triggered checks after a first draft.
